title: Bonhoeffer's end (1945)
hookLine: executed weeks before liberation; his prison letters still read worldwide

lines: GET READY TO COME WITH US.
A SUNDAY SERVICE IN A SCHOOLROOM.
cards: Prisoner Bonhoeffer, get ready to come with us. That, by one account, is what the guards said at the door of a schoolroom where a group of prisoners was being held near the end of the war.

The pastor had just led a short Sunday service for the others. He took a book, wrote his name in it, and asked one of the men, a British officer, to carry a message to a friend in England if he could.
Then he went with the guards. The officer remembered the message.

teach.b: Bonhoeffer was arrested at his parents' house in Berlin and held for a long time in a military prison.

Through family and friends he had become connected to people plotting against Hitler, and after a failed attempt on Hitler's life, those connections were uncovered. Christians still talk about this honestly.

A man who wrote about following Jesus, and was drawn toward peace, joined in some way a conspiracy to kill a tyrant. Some see costly obedience in an impossible time. Others hold it as a hard question that doesn't resolve.
In prison he wrote letters to his parents, to his fiancée, Maria, and to his closest friend, Eberhard Bethge, who later gathered them into a book.
They're full of ordinary things, a request for books, thanks for a parcel, and full of big questions about God and faith in a world that seemed to go on without either. He wrote poems too.

teach.h: WHO AM I? A QUESTION GIVEN TO GOD.
teach.b: In one he asks who he really is, the calm man the guards see or the restless one he knows inside, and ends by placing the question with God.
Near the end he was moved to the concentration camp at Flossenbürg and hanged there, shortly before the war in Europe ended. The message the officer carried was short.

teach.h: THE END, THE BEGINNING OF LIFE.
teach.b: As he remembered it, Bonhoeffer said: this is the end, for me the beginning of life.
It echoes an old Christian hope, which Paul puts this way in the King James Bible: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?"
The letters are still read today, for their honesty, even by people who share none of his faith.

how: Bonhoeffer is remembered on the calendars of several churches, including Lutheran and Anglican ones, and his prison letters and poems are read in study groups, sermons and private devotion.

games.q: you're a pastor in a prison cell, with paper and a pencil and no idea how long you have. what do you write?
o: a formal last testament and nothing else.
letters home, ordinary things and big questions together.
nothing, in case it's read by the guards.
games.why: Bonhoeffer wrote letters to family, his fiancée and his friend, full of small news and deep questions, plus poems. they're still read.

practice: Start a letter in your head to someone far away, by distance, by time or by a falling-out.

Bonhoeffer's letters mixed small news with big things, so begin with something ordinary, what you ate, what you're reading, then add one sentence that matters. If you pray, pray for them as you write it.

wordCard.voice: Bonhoeffer's end. A pastor executed by the Nazi state, who left behind prison letters and, by one account, called his death the beginning of life.

orig.note: Greek: life, the word in John 11:25, I am the resurrection, and the life.
